Recovery potential depends on timing, payment method, beneficiary account status, availability of a chargeback/recall mechanism and jurisdiction. Examples worth examining are recent transfers, card disputes with an applicable scheme route, confirmed mistaken recipient details, fraud proceeds traceable at another institution and assets subject to lawful freezing/recovery. Recovery is never automatically guaranteed. Recovery channels in the guide include rapid payment recall, interbank coordination and requests, account restrictions/freezing where permitted, card chargeback routes, reversal/return mechanisms, reimbursement/indemnity under applicable rules, and legal/civil recovery where proportionate. overviewSections.heading: Apply the concepts
overviewSections.text: Liability is rule-dependent, not an absolute division. Chip-and-PIN cases turn on authorization/authentication evidence, cardholder protections and local/card-scheme rules. CNP disputes depend on authentication, scheme chargeback allocation and merchant/issuer evidence. Never assume the merchant or bank always bears every loss. A fraud-incident report documents what occurred, impact, facts and control actions for internal governance/authorized stakeholders. A SAR/STR is a specific regulatory suspicious-activity disclosure to the appropriate FIU or competent authority via the entity's approved escalation and filing process; suspected fraud does not mechanically mean the investigator personally files one. Useful fraud KPIs include total loss, gross exposure, recovered funds, alert/true-positive performance, false-positive rate, detection time, response or investigation timeliness, customer impact and remediation effectiveness. recallAnswers: Eight steps: DEFINE requirements → ACQUIRE/PREPARE data → ENGINEER features → SELECT model → TRAIN → EVALUATE → DEPLOY → MONITOR and refine. Decide required fraud outcome and data quality before fitting a model.

PRECISION = TP/(TP+FP): fraction of flagged cases truly fraudulent. RECALL = TP/(TP+FN): fraction of actual fraud detected. Recall answers 'how much real fraud did we find?'; precision answers 'how trustworthy are our alerts?'.

When fraud is rare, a model can predict 'legitimate' for almost all transactions and achieve very high overall accuracy while missing most fraud. Evaluate confusion-matrix metrics (recall, precision, false positives, F1 and other appropriate measures), not accuracy alone.

BAGGING trains models on resampled datasets and aggregates outputs, generally reducing variance. BOOSTING trains models sequentially to correct earlier errors. STACKING combines outputs of several models via a meta-model. Choose based on validation, complexity and stability.

CNNs are most associated with image/spatial patterns; RNNs with sequences or time-dependent data. Fraud applications depend on task design; the comparison is a model-family memory aid, not a rule for every architecture.

TRAINING data fits model parameters. VALIDATION data supports tuning, feature and threshold selection. TEST data remains held out until final generalization assessment. Avoid leakage of future events or shared linked records across splits.

Lowering an alert threshold usually increases sensitivity/recall (more fraud caught), but often increases false positives, workload and customer friction. Check the precision–recall balance and risk appetite before changing the threshold.

BACKTESTING applies proposed rules/model to historical transactions. OUT-OF-SAMPLE testing evaluates new data excluded from development; STRESS testing examines extreme/adversarial conditions, load or unusual behaviors. Each addresses a different failure mode.

For identity-proofing, focus on collecting claimed identity, validating document/data authenticity, checking against trusted sources, binding the individual to the claim, and applying appropriate authentication/ongoing checks. Useful data validation checks include completeness, accuracy, consistency/format, and timeliness or freshness. Confirm transaction IDs, missing values, currency/timezone normalization and label integrity before training fraud models.

Bias controls include representative training data, feature/label quality checks, fairness testing across appropriate segments, transparent review of outcomes and periodic retraining/governance. Verify any tradeoff against both fraud detection and consumer fairness.

recallAnswers: PHISHING = deceptive email. VISHING = deceptive voice call. SMISHING = deceptive text message. SPEAR PHISHING = personalized targeting. EMPLOYEE TARGETING focuses staff with useful access. BEC/CEO FRAUD impersonates an executive or known business counterpart, often seeking an urgent secret payment or changed payee.

APP fraud relies on persuading the victim to AUTHORIZE a payment. MALICIOUS PAYEE: payment for fake/nonexistent goods or services; MALICIOUS REDIRECTION: payment diverted using impersonation or changed account instructions. The memorisation guide discusses instant/real-time payment contexts; examples vary by jurisdiction, so distinguish mechanism from the name of a payment system.

Social engineering manipulates trust, fear, greed or authority. Techniques include PRETEXTING (false story), BAITING (tempting offer), QUID PRO QUO (service for information), IMPERSONATION, and TAILGATING (gaining access by following authorized users). Examples: fake bank fraud-team calls and executive payment requests.

Account takeover can follow phishing/vishing, malware, credential leaks, SIM swaps or social engineering. Clues: unfamiliar device/geolocation, contact details changed, new payees, password reset followed quickly by unusual transfers.

Identity-fraud clues can include a mismatch between applicant identity and records, inconsistent address/document information, thin or implausible history, shared device/contact across unrelated identities, and unusual attempts at account/credit creation. Corroborate; no single clue proves identity theft.

PONZI pays earlier investors from new investors' funds. PYRAMID depends chiefly on recruiting participants. BOILER ROOM uses high-pressure investment sales. PIG BUTCHERING builds relationship and trust before pushing fraudulent investments. FRAUD AS A SERVICE supplies tools/infrastructure to enable scams; it is not a specific investment return structure.

Advance-fee examples: lottery prize fees, inheritance/unclaimed funds, fake employment placement, visa processing, loan approvals, debt elimination and fraudulent recovery services. The common feature is a payment demanded before an attractive promised benefit.

CNP clues: many small test purchases, rapid successive declines/authorizations, atypical time or country, mismatched billing/shipping address, new delivery address and sudden unusual-value purchases. CNP does not require a physical cloned card.

A deliberate chargeback/friendly fraud involves intentionally disputing a valid purchase. Accidental chargebacks can result from failure to recognize a legitimate descriptor; they are not automatically dishonest. Investigate intent, transaction evidence and merchant/issuer records instead of assuming all disputes are fraud.

Application fraud methods include falsely declared income/employment, concealed liabilities, forged supporting documents, or use of stolen/synthetic identities. Red flags: inconsistent application data, edited payslips/bank statements, reused digital identifiers or improbable credit history. Origination fraud occurs at relationship formation.

Money mule types: UNWITTING genuinely unaware; WITTING/WILLFULLY BLIND notices signs but ignores them; COMPLICIT knowingly participates. The party classification in the supplied guide places intentional money muling as second-party and manipulated unintentional muling as third-party.

PHANTOM VENDOR: fabricated supplier and sham invoice receiving payments. GHOST EMPLOYEE: fictitious payroll person receiving salary. Both may exploit weak onboarding, master-data review and segregation of duties, but affect different expense streams.

Internal fraud signs include privileged unusual access, unexplained lifestyle pressure, refusal to share duties, vendor favoritism or suspicious overrides. Controls include segregation/four-eyes review, independent reconciliation, access management, KYE, whistleblower channels and audits.

PHYSICAL asset misappropriation: stolen inventory, equipment or company property. FINANCIAL asset misappropriation: diverting payments, embezzlement or false expenses. Fraudulent financial reporting manipulates statements and disclosures rather than simply taking an asset.

Financial statement methods: fictitious sales, early/inflated revenue, inflated assets, hidden liabilities, deferred expenses and misleading disclosures. Clues: unsupported journals, unusual end-period changes, inconsistencies with cash/operations and override of financial controls. Treat red flags as hypotheses to test.

BRIBERY: benefit exchanged for improper action. CORRUPTION: broader abuse of delegated power, which may include bribery, influence peddling and graft. EMBEZZLEMENT: misappropriation of entrusted funds/assets. GRAFT: illicit gain from improper exploitation of a position.

A COUNTERFEIT document imitates a genuine document but was not issued by the claimed authority. A FORGED document alters or falsely signs an authentic or purported record. Examine issuing source, security features, metadata and inconsistencies before classification.

Authenticity questions: Who actually issued it? Does it match reliable independent records? Are the format/security features and chronology credible? Red flags include altered dates, inconsistent fonts/number formats, implausible seals, poor alignment, mismatched IDs and contradictory content.

flashcards.back: TP / (TP + FP): of alerts labeled fraud, fraction that truly is fraud.
flashcards.source: Module 2 memorisation guide, Ch 4; study guide Module 2 §§72–101

study.meaning: TP / (TP + FP): of alerts labeled fraud, fraction that truly is fraud.
study.context: PRECISION = TP/(TP+FP): fraction of flagged cases truly fraudulent. RECALL = TP/(TP+FN): fraction of actual fraud detected. Recall answers 'how much real fraud did we find?'; precision answers 'how trustworthy are our alerts?'.
study.example: An alert system flags 30 transactions, but 15 are fraud: precision = 15/30 = 50%.
study.distinction: Precision asks what proportion of the alerts were genuine; recall asks how many real frauds were detected.
study.reference: Module 2 memorisation guide, Ch 4; study guide Module 2 §§72–101

flashcards.back: TP / (TP + FN): of actual fraud, fraction identified by the detection model.
flashcards.source: Module 2 memorisation guide, Ch 4; study guide Module 2 §§72–101

study.meaning: TP / (TP + FN): of actual fraud, fraction identified by the detection model.
study.context: PRECISION = TP/(TP+FP): fraction of flagged cases truly fraudulent. RECALL = TP/(TP+FN): fraction of actual fraud detected. Recall answers 'how much real fraud did we find?'; precision answers 'how trustworthy are our alerts?'.
study.example: If 20 real frauds occurred and the system found 15, recall = 15/20 = 75%.
study.distinction: Recall concerns false negatives (missed fraud); precision concerns false positives in flagged cases.
study.reference: Module 2 memorisation guide, Ch 4; study guide Module 2 §§72–101

flashcards.back: Legitimate events erroneously flagged; excess generates customer friction.
flashcards.source: Module 2 memorisation guide, Ch 4; study guide Module 2 §§72–101

study.meaning: Legitimate events erroneously flagged; excess generates customer friction.
study.context: Lowering an alert threshold usually increases sensitivity/recall (more fraud caught), but often increases false positives, workload and customer friction. Check the precision–recall balance and risk appetite before changing the threshold.
study.example: A system wrongly flags 20 genuine transactions among 980 legitimate: FPR = 20/980.
study.distinction: False positive rate = FP/(FP+TN); do not confuse with false discovery among alerts (1 − precision).
study.reference: Module 2 memorisation guide, Ch 4; study guide Module 2 §§72–101

flashcards.back: Organizes TP, FP, TN and FN to assess fraud classification performance.
flashcards.source: Module 2 memorisation guide, Ch 4; study guide Module 2 §§72–101

study.meaning: Organizes TP, FP, TN and FN to assess fraud classification performance.
study.context: When fraud is rare, a model can predict 'legitimate' for almost all transactions and achieve very high overall accuracy while missing most fraud. Evaluate confusion-matrix metrics (recall, precision, false positives, F1 and other appropriate measures), not accuracy alone.
study.example: Of 1,000 payments, 20 are fraud; 15 flagged correctly, 5 missed, 15 genuine incorrectly flagged, 965 genuine cleared.
study.distinction: TP=fraud flagged, FP=genuine flagged, TN=genuine cleared, FN=fraud missed.
study.reference: Module 2 memorisation guide, Ch 4; study guide Module 2 §§72–101

study.meaning: Be empathetic, nonjudgmental, prepared and clear about next steps.
study.context: Prepare before contact, use one or two responsible contacts, speak empathetically and without blame, use clear language, allow time for questions, establish follow-up expectations and use lawful support/escalation channels. A romance/APP victim may initially trust the fraudster.
study.reference: Module 3 memorisation guide, Ch 1; study guide Module 3 §§6–24

flashcards.source: Module 3 memorisation guide, Ch 1; study guide Module 3 §§6–24

study.meaning: Coordinate fraud, cyber, AML, legal and HR specialists as facts require.
study.context: Joint investigations commonly have a coordinated financial-crime or designated central lead, with cyber, AML/FIU, HR, legal and business units contributing evidence. Formal SAR/STR filing follows the entity's authorized AML/FIU reporting process and local law, not automatic action by every investigator.
study.reference: Module 3 memorisation guide, Ch 1; study guide Module 3 §§6–24

flashcards.back: Defines roles, stakeholders and communication during an incident.
flashcards.source: Module 3 memorisation guide, Ch 1; study guide Module 3 §§6–24

study.meaning: Defines roles, stakeholders and communication during an incident.
study.context: Five investigation-plan stages: CASE CREATION, INITIAL REVIEW/ANALYSIS (including urgent interim action), STAKEHOLDER NOTIFICATION, EVIDENCE-BASED INVESTIGATION, and CONCLUSION/INTELLIGENCE SHARING. Preserve evidence and follow SLAs throughout.
study.reference: Module 3 memorisation guide, Ch 1; study guide Module 3 §§6–24

flashcards.source: Module 3 memorisation guide, Ch 2; study guide Module 3 §§25–57

study.meaning: Victim authorizes payment under deception; not the same as stolen-login ATO.
study.context: APP fraud relies on persuading the victim to AUTHORIZE a payment. MALICIOUS PAYEE: payment for fake/nonexistent goods or services; MALICIOUS REDIRECTION: payment diverted using impersonation or changed account instructions. The memorisation guide discusses instant/real-time payment contexts; examples vary by jurisdiction, so distinguish mechanism from the name of a payment system.
study.distinction: Victim authorizes the transfer under deception; account takeover involves unauthorized account control.

flashcards.source: Module 3 memorisation guide, Ch 2; study guide Module 3 §§25–57

study.meaning: Existing investor returns are paid from capital supplied by later investors.
study.context: PONZI pays earlier investors from new investors' funds. PYRAMID depends chiefly on recruiting participants. BOILER ROOM uses high-pressure investment sales. PIG BUTCHERING builds relationship and trust before pushing fraudulent investments. FRAUD AS A SERVICE supplies tools/infrastructure to enable scams; it is not a specific investment return structure.
study.example: New investor deposits are used to make promised payouts to earlier investors.
study.distinction: Ponzi pays prior investors from later investments, whereas a pyramid primarily rewards recruitment.

study.distinction: Pyramid depends on recruiting participants, not a supposedly managed investment return stream.

flashcards.source: Module 3 memorisation guide, Ch 2; study guide Module 3 §§25–57

study.meaning: Victim pays a fee for a promised benefit that never arrives.
study.context: Advance-fee examples: lottery prize fees, inheritance/unclaimed funds, fake employment placement, visa processing, loan approvals, debt elimination and fraudulent recovery services. The common feature is a payment demanded before an attractive promised benefit.
study.reference: Module 3 memorisation guide, Ch 2; study guide Module 3 §§25–57

flashcards.back: Small card tests, new delivery address, rapid attempted transactions and unusual location.
flashcards.source: Module 3 memorisation guide, Ch 2; study guide Module 3 §§25–57

study.meaning: Small card tests, new delivery address, rapid attempted transactions and unusual location.
study.context: CNP clues: many small test purchases, rapid successive declines/authorizations, atypical time or country, mismatched billing/shipping address, new delivery address and sudden unusual-value purchases. CNP does not require a physical cloned card.
study.reference: Module 3 memorisation guide, Ch 2; study guide Module 3 §§25–57

flashcards.back: A fraudulent vendor identity diverts invoice payments.
flashcards.source: Module 3 memorisation guide, Ch 2; study guide Module 3 §§25–57

study.meaning: A fraudulent vendor identity diverts invoice payments.
study.context: PHANTOM VENDOR: fabricated supplier and sham invoice receiving payments. GHOST EMPLOYEE: fictitious payroll person receiving salary. Both may exploit weak onboarding, master-data review and segregation of duties, but affect different expense streams.
study.example: Accounts payable receives invoices from a nonexistent supplier secretly created by an employee.
study.distinction: Phantom vendor is a fake supplier; ghost employee is a fake payroll entry.
study.reference: Module 3 memorisation guide, Ch 2; study guide Module 3 §§25–57

flashcards.back: A fictitious payroll entry diverts salary payments.
flashcards.source: Module 3 memorisation guide, Ch 2; study guide Module 3 §§25–57

study.meaning: A fictitious payroll entry diverts salary payments.
study.context: PHANTOM VENDOR: fabricated supplier and sham invoice receiving payments. GHOST EMPLOYEE: fictitious payroll person receiving salary. Both may exploit weak onboarding, master-data review and segregation of duties, but affect different expense streams.
study.example: Payroll continues paying a fictitious staff profile into an insider-controlled account.
study.distinction: Ghost employee targets payroll; phantom vendor targets accounts payable/procurement.
study.reference: Module 3 memorisation guide, Ch 2; study guide Module 3 §§25–57

flashcards.back: Suspects criminality but intentionally ignores warning signs.
flashcards.source: Module 3 memorisation guide, Ch 2; study guide Module 3 §§25–57

study.meaning: Suspects criminality but intentionally ignores warning signs.
study.context: Money mule types: UNWITTING genuinely unaware; WITTING/WILLFULLY BLIND notices signs but ignores them; COMPLICIT knowingly participates. The party classification in the supplied guide places intentional money muling as second-party and manipulated unintentional muling as third-party.
study.reference: Module 3 memorisation guide, Ch 2; study guide Module 3 §§25–57

flashcards.source: Module 3 memorisation guide, Ch 2; study guide Module 3 §§25–57

study.meaning: Intentional distortion of reporting, unlike direct asset misappropriation.
study.context: Financial statement methods: fictitious sales, early/inflated revenue, inflated assets, hidden liabilities, deferred expenses and misleading disclosures. Clues: unsupported journals, unusual end-period changes, inconsistencies with cash/operations and override of financial controls. Treat red flags as hypotheses to test.
study.reference: Module 3 memorisation guide, Ch 2; study guide Module 3 §§25–57

flashcards.source: Module 3 memorisation guide, Ch 3; study guide Module 3 §§59–82

study.meaning: Chronological record of evidence collection, access, transfers and handling.
study.context: CHAIN OF CUSTODY logs who acquired, accessed, handled, copied or transferred evidence and when, preserving integrity and evidential value. Lawful seizure of evidence from external parties normally involves authorized law enforcement or legal process, not unilateral action by a bank investigator.
study.example: Log the analyst who collected CCTV footage, the time obtained and every subsequent transfer.
study.distinction: The record of who handled evidence is part of proving it remained reliable.
study.reference: Module 3 memorisation guide, Ch 3; study guide Module 3 §§59–82

flashcards.source: Module 3 memorisation guide, Ch 3; study guide Module 3 §§59–82

study.meaning: Follow originating, intermediary and beneficiary institutions or account flows.
study.context: The classic laundering stages are PLACEMENT (introduce funds), LAYERING (obscure source with movements), INTEGRATION (appear legitimate). Examples of concerns: unusually structured deposits, rapid circuitous transfers, then apparently legitimate investment/purchase. These are AML concepts supporting fraud-proceeds tracing.

flashcards.back: Underlying failure or weakness allowing fraud, distinct from the scheme label.
flashcards.source: Module 3 memorisation guide, Ch 3; study guide Module 3 §§59–82

study.meaning: Underlying failure or weakness allowing fraud, distinct from the scheme label.
study.context: Root cause analysis reconstructs incident facts, identifies the failed or absent controls, investigates why they failed, tests contributing factors, then assigns corrective actions and measures effectiveness. 'Phishing' names the fraud method; 'missing second-factor verification' may be a control root cause.
study.example: A stolen-credential fraud succeeded because a new-payee change had no step-up verification.
study.distinction: A typology says HOW the offender acted; root cause asks WHY controls failed.
study.reference: Module 3 memorisation guide, Ch 3; study guide Module 3 §§59–82

flashcards.back: Ask nonleading questions that permit a witness's own account.
flashcards.source: Module 3 memorisation guide, Ch 3; study guide Module 3 §§59–82

study.meaning: Ask nonleading questions that permit a witness's own account.
study.context: Plan interviews, review existing records first, then speak with victims/whistleblowers/witnesses as appropriate before potentially implicated subjects so testimony is not inadvertently contaminated. Actual order is situation- and law-dependent; preserve witness safety and confidentiality.
study.example: “Tell me what happened after you received the call,” rather than “The caller asked for your OTP, didn’t they?”
study.distinction: A leading question implies an answer; open-ended questions elicit an unprompted account.
study.reference: Module 3 memorisation guide, Ch 3; study guide Module 3 §§59–82

flashcards.back: Conclusions should follow documented, credible evidence and applicable standards.
flashcards.source: Module 3 memorisation guide, Ch 4; study guide Module 3 §§84–103

study.meaning: Conclusions should follow documented, credible evidence and applicable standards.
study.context: For closure, examine whether factual findings are sufficiently supported, investigative actions and approvals are recorded, regulatory/customer obligations are considered, and disposition/next steps are documented. A suspicion alone is not equivalent to a proven offense.
study.example: A single unusual login is a clue; supported case findings require corroborated logs, transactions and relevant statements.
study.distinction: An alert or red flag is not alone sufficient proof of fraud.

study.context: When fraud is supported by evidence, determine immediate protective/account action, evaluate recovery and reporting duties, and document a reasoned disposition plus control recommendations. Coordinate appropriate customer communication and management approval.
